name: Powdered pearl
lead: Powdered pearl, or pearl powder (zhenzhu fen), is finely ground pearl or nacre (mother-of-pearl), composed mainly of calcium carbonate with an organic protein matrix. It is a traditional Chinese medicine ingredient with a documented use of roughly two thousand years, applied to the skin or taken by mouth for complexion and general health.[1][2][11]

People use it to get a brighter, smoother, more luminous-looking complexion: as a mask or cream ingredient applied to the face, and as an oral powder or capsule taken for skin. Wikipedia says it is widely believed to improve the appearance of skin, has been used as a cosmetic by royal families in Asia and is used for acne.[11] Traditional texts also describe it as fading dark spots and sun damage.[11]

Published research is mostly laboratory, animal and biomaterials work on wound healing and bone repair, including cell studies of pearl-derived protein on pigment pathways and a mouse study of pearl extract on UV-induced photoaging, plus a few small human studies of other outcomes. A narrative review describes the evidence base as lacking in-depth understanding despite the long history of use.[2][12][13] No trial of pearl powder for complexion or skin lightening in people has been published.

paras: Pearl powder is made by grinding pearls into small grains, whereas nacre powder comes from the inner shell layer. Pearls form when an irritant lodges in an oyster and is coated with nacre.[3] The mineral phase is mainly calcium carbonate, held in a framework of organic molecules including water-soluble matrix proteins, which researchers consider important to its biological activity.[1][3] Nacre and pearl extracts are more commonly reported than pearl itself because pearls are expensive and limited in supply.[3]

Wikipedia dates use in China to at least 320 AD for both medicine and cosmetics, and says Empress Wu Zetian (625-705 AD) reportedly used it internally and on her skin. In the Ming dynasty the Bencao Gangmu credited pearl with promoting skin growth, releasing toxins and fading sun damage and age spots.[11]

The article also records use elsewhere: the Kashmiri physician Narahari described it in about 1240 as an antidote and remedy, European physicians used it in attempts to treat Charles VI of France and Lorenzo de Medici, Francis Bacon suggested it could prolong life, and in the nineteenth century women used it as a skin whitener, although an 1838 source criticised it for leaving a sickly pallor.[11] The article notes that its own medical and some historical claims need stronger sourcing.[11]

In traditional Chinese medicine pearl is credited with calming the mind, clearing the eyes and detoxifying the muscle, and pearl powder is used for beauty care as well as health indications.[2][3] Wikipedia lists anti-inflammatory, detoxifying and relaxant roles, and says some studies claim stimulation of skin fibroblasts, collagen regeneration and quicker healing of wounds and burns.[11] Wikipedia notes pearl powder contains amino acids, over 30 trace minerals and a high concentration of calcium, and that a traditional oral amount is about one gram in water or tea twice weekly; excessive doses may cause calcium toxicity.[11]

A 2021 review lists wound healing, bone repair and treatment of skin conditions among its emerging biomedical applications.[2] Pearl-derived hydrolysed conchiolin protein has been reported in a 2023 laboratory paper to counter both endothelin-1 and alpha-MSH signalling, two pathways involved in pigmentation, for skin whitening,[12] and a 2022 study in mice reported a protective effect of pearl extract against UV-induced photoaging.[13] These are not human complexion trials.
No studies found testing pearl powder for skin brightening or complexion in humans. Human research on pearl-derived products addresses other outcomes.

A randomised, placebo-controlled trial of protein-rich pearl powder examined antioxidant status in a small group of volunteers, alongside laboratory work.[4] A pilot randomised trial gave bio-calcium from Pinctada maxima shell to postmenopausal women with reduced bone mineral density,[5] and a study assessed calcium bioavailability of nano-sized pearl powder in adults.[6] A case report described a 94-year-old woman with a stage 2 pressure injury treated with a metronidazole and nano pearl powder mixture.[7] Two registered trials compare pearl powder with CPP-ACP for enamel white spot lesions.[8][9]

Most remaining work is preclinical. A 2026 narrative review found pearl-specific studies generally support osteogenic activity in cell, scaffold and defect models, while noting heterogeneity and limited direct evidence on high-dose toxicity or heavy-metal risk.[10]

Laboratory work supports the cosmetic hypothesis only indirectly: a cell-based report on pearl-derived conchiolin protein and pigment signalling,[12] and a mouse photoaging study.[13] Human skin outcomes have not been tested in a published trial.

A 2026 review notes that pearl-specific literature offers limited direct evidence on chronic biosafety, immunogenicity or heavy-metal-related risk of nano-pearl powder.[10] No safety data for cosmetic or oral use for complexion have been published.

card.summary: Ground pearl used in Chinese medicine for a luminous complexion; research covers wound and bone repair, not skin brightening.
card.note: No human trials for skin brightening; long-term safety data are limited.

quick.overview:
Powdered pearl is finely ground pearl or mother-of-pearl, a traditional Chinese medicine used for over two thousand years in beauty and health preparations. It is sold as a topical mask ingredient and as an oral powder.
Modern research mostly covers wound healing and bone repair in laboratory and animal models, with a few small human studies on other outcomes. No trial tests it for complexion or skin brightening.
quick.mechanism: Pearl is mostly calcium carbonate with a protein matrix. Researchers attribute antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair activity mainly to the water-soluble matrix proteins, studied in cells and animals.
quick.risks: Reviews say direct evidence on long-term safety, heavy-metal content and immune effects is limited. No safety data specific to cosmetic use are available.

angle.text: Pearl powder is mixed into masks and creams or taken orally for a brighter, more luminous complexion. The link to appearance rests on traditional use and on laboratory work on pigment and repair pathways.
